The expulsion of the Portuguese from the “natural boundary” was the result of a formal, state‑led removal that followed the old,
geographic frontiers established by the Iberian treaties. The natural boundary in question ran along the **Guadiana River**, which, for centuries, had defined the border between **Portugal** (the country that had hosted the particular tournament) and its neighbour **Spain**, where “A Don” (the town or area in question) lies.

After the **Treaty of Tordesillas** and a series of subsequent Iberian agreements, the Guadiana became a recognized natural border. In the mid‑18th century, the Portuguese monarchy, under the influence of the Jesuit suppression and the political climate of the time, enacted a decree that forcibly expelled Portuguese citizens, particularly members of the Jesuit order, from all holdings on the Spanish side of the Guadiana. The removal was carried out by Portuguese troops and officials with orders from the king and the court, who crossed the river, seized properties, and expelled the Portuguese residents. This operation was part of a larger effort to reinforce the political and religious divisions that the natural border had long symbolised.

steps.text:
The expulsion of the Portuguese from the “natural boundary” was the result of a formal, state‑led removal that followed the old,
geographic frontiers established by the Iberian treaties. The natural boundary in question ran along the **Guadiana River**, which, for centuries, had defined the border between **Portugal** (the country that had hosted the particular tournament) and its neighbour **Spain**, where “A Don” (the town or area in question) lies.

After the **Treaty of Tordesillas** and a series of subsequent Iberian agreements, the Guadiana became a recognized natural border. In the mid‑18th century, the Portuguese monarchy, under the influence of the Jesuit suppression and the political climate of the time, enacted a decree that forcibly expelled Portuguese citizens, particularly members of the Jesuit order, from all holdings on the Spanish side of the Guadiana. The removal was carried out by Portuguese troops and officials with orders from the king and the court, who crossed the river, seized properties, and expelled the Portuguese residents. This operation was part of a larger effort to reinforce the political and religious divisions that the natural border had long symbolised.
